name: Amariah
title: High Priest under Jehoshaphat and Chief Judge in Spiritual Matters
summary: Amarja served as high priest in the kingdom of Judah during King Jehoshaphat's reign (c. 872–848 B.C.). As a central part of Jehoshaphat's comprehensive legal reform, Amarja was given authority over all religious and spiritual cases, while Shebajah ben Ishmael, the leader of the tribe of Judah, was made responsible for civil matters. This division of judicial authority represents an early and remarkable example of institutional separation of powers in Israel's history. The name Amarja (Hebrew: Amaryah) means "Yahweh has spoken" or "Yahweh has promised," and is borne by several other persons in the Old Testament, including priests listed in genealogies and an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah.

keyEvents.title: Appointed as Chief Judge in Spiritual Matters
keyEvents.description: King Jehoshaphat appointed Amarjah as high priest to lead in all matters concerning the Lord, as part of a comprehensive judicial reform in Judah.

keyEvents.title: Jehoshaphat's Judicial Reform
keyEvents.description: Jehoshaphat appointed judges throughout the land and established a higher court in Jerusalem. Amarjah led the religious cases, while Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the leader of the tribe of Judah, was responsible for civil matters. The Levites served as scribes in the court.

keyEvents.title: Amarjah in the Genealogy of the Priests
keyEvents.description: The name Amariah appears at least twice in the genealogy of the high priests in 1 Chronicles – as a son of Meremoth and as a son of Azariah. These are likely different individuals from the high priest under Jehoshaphat, but they demonstrate the continuity of the priesthood through generations.

keyEvents.title: Amarjah Among Those Who Sealed the Covenant
keyEvents.description: Another person named Amariah is mentioned among the priests who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah after returning from exile in Babylon. This is likely a different person than the high priest during Jehoshaphat.

keyEvents.title: Amariah in Zephaniah's genealogy
keyEvents.description: The prophet Zephaniah is identified as a descendant of an Amariah, who was the son of Hezekiah. If this Hezekiah is King Hezekiah, it links the prophet to the royal line. This Amariah is probably a different person than the high priest during Jehoshaphat.

versions.summary: Amariah was a high priest who served under King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He was appointed to lead in all spiritual and religious matters and played an important role in Jehoshaphat's judicial reform. The name Amariah means 'the Lord has said' or 'the Lord has promised,' and several people in the Bible bear this name.

footnotes.text: The name Amariah (Hebrew: אֲמַרְיָה, Amaryah) is composed of the Hebrew verb 'amar' (to say/speak) and the shortened form of God's name 'Yah,' thus meaning 'Yahweh has spoken' or 'Yahweh has promised.'

Jehoshaphat's judicial reform, described in 2 Chronicles 19, is one of the most detailed accounts of the legal system in ancient Israel. The division into a court for religious matters under the high priest and one for civil matters under a royal official reflects an early form of institutional separation of powers that is rarely documented in the ancient Near East.

There are at least six or seven different people named Amariah in the Old Testament, distributed among priests, Levites, and royal descendants. The name's prevalence testifies to its popularity as a theophoric personal name in ancient Israel.

In rabbinic tradition, Jehoshaphat's judicial reform has been interpreted as a model for the later Sanhedrin system. Tosefta Sanhedrin discusses similar principles for organizing religious and legal courts under the high priest.

Archaeological findings from the Kingdom of Judah in the 9th century BCE, including administrative seals and ostraca, confirm a period of increased bureaucratization and centralization that aligns with the biblical account of Jehoshaphat's reforms.

Shebaja ben Ishmael, who according to 2 Chron. 19:11 was given responsibility for civil matters, is referred to as 'leader of the house of Judah.' This division between religious and secular authority represents an important principle in Israelite governance.
